caution: A failure to reproduce is not a finding that the paper is wrong. It may be a failure of the attempt.

attempts.label: DANDI:001425
attempts.paper_title: A multimodal dataset linking wide-field calcium imaging to behavior changes in mice during an operant lever-pull task

inputs.what: Names of the body-camera keypoints (rightbartip is "The tip of the lever", leftbartip "The tip of the pawrest") and the unit of the lever channel (mm), from bdbc_nwb_explorer/data/body_video.csv and data/daq.csv. Used only to name a keypoint and a unit the dataset already holds; no measurement comes from it.

attempts.entry_title: Wide-field calcium imaging and behaviour in the BraiDyn-BC lever-pull task (Kondo et al. 2025)
attempts.summary: Most of the paper's main findings held up in this data. The response rate to the tone rose over training (median 0.556 to 0.856), the mice split into two clusters by their final pull duration, visual and whisker responses peaked in right VISp and left barrel cortex, and the tracked lever tip followed the encoder. Whether the success rate stayed constant, and matched between clusters late in training, could not be tested, because the paper gives no test and the readings disagree. The Figure 6 statements on movement order and on areas tracking the pupil could not be tested, as the example session is not identified. The landmark and DeepLabCut validations need manual annotations that are not deposited.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Kondo, Sehara, Harukuni, Aoki et al. (2025) on dandiset 001425, which holds wide-field calcium imaging, behavioural sensors and video keypoints from 25 mice over 15 sessions of a cued lever-pull task, with resting-state and sensory-mapping sessions. It checks the session and cohort counts, the learning curves and the clustering of mice by required pull duration, the stability of the fluorescence, the sensory maps, the absence of aberrant transients, the correlation of video keypoints with the lever, and the pull-aligned activity and movements.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Kondo et al. (2025) from dandiset 001425

outcomes.statement: The dataset comes from 25 mice of both sexes, 11 males and 14 females, aged 17 to 31 weeks at the end of the experiments.
outcomes.quote: The mice of both sexes (11 males and 14 females) were used for the experiments. The age ranged from 17–31 weeks at the end of experiments.
outcomes.notes: 25 subjects, 11 male and 14 female. Age at each subject's last session (a sensory-mapping session) is 16.3 to 31.6 weeks from the date of birth and from the age field alike, inside the widened range of 15.3 to 34.1 weeks. One mouse (VG1-GC#87) is 16.3 weeks, below the paper's 17.

outcomes.statement: Of the 375 task training sessions (25 mice by 15 sessions), data were collected from 364 (97%); the 11 others lacked complete imaging. All 15 sessions were collected for 16 of the 25 mice.
outcomes.source: Background & Summary, paragraph 3; Technical Validation, paragraph 2; Figure 3d legend
outcomes.quote: Of the 375 task training sessions conducted, we successfully collected data from 364 sessions ( Fig. 3d ; Table 1 ) and completed data collection for all 15 sessions in 16 out of 25 animals.
outcomes.notes: 364 distinct task sessions (file name and session description agree), 16 mice with all 15. The 11 missing sessions are listed per mouse. No recording was found deposited twice. The dataset also holds 98 resting-state sessions (VG1-GC#119 and VG1-GC#122 lack day 15) and 33 sensory-mapping sessions, 8 mice having two.

outcomes.statement: Each task session was imaged for 30 min (108000 frames at 60 Hz, so 54000 frames per excitation channel at 30 Hz), each resting-state session for 10 min and the sensory-mapping session for 15 min.
outcomes.source: Methods, Acquisition of wide-field one-photon image, paragraph 1; Data Records, Imaging Raw Data
outcomes.quote: We imaged 108000 frames (30 min) in each task session, 36000 frames in each resting-state session (10 min on recording days 1, 7, 15), and 54000 frames in the sensory mapping session (recording day 16).
outcomes.notes: 363 of 364 task sessions have 54000 frames per channel, all 98 resting-state sessions 18000, and 29 of 33 sensory-mapping sessions 27000, for the dF/F and both raw stacks. The exceptions are one task session of 45413 frames (VG1-GC#124 day 5, noted in the file as recorded for 25.2 min) and four sensory-mapping sessions of 36000 frames (VG1-GC#48, VG1-GC#63, VG1-GC#66, VG1-GC#73, day 16).

outcomes.statement: Training had 3.1 +/- 0.6 breaks per mouse of 2.3 +/- 0.7 days each (mean +/- s.d., 25 mice), and recording days 1 to 16 spanned 24.28 +/- 3.2 calendar days.
outcomes.quote: There were occasional training breaks of typically 2–3 days without any handling ( e.g. over weekends; 3.1 ± 0.6 breaks throughout training; 2.3 ± 0.7 days per break; mean ± s.d., n = 25 mice). ... The entire recording period (recording day 1 to 16) spanned 24.28 ± 3.2 calendar days (mean ± s.d.).
outcomes.notes: Under every reading the means are within the paper's s.d. Breaks per mouse are 3.28 (breaks of one or more days) or 2.84 (two or more days), 2.80 to 3.28 across readings; days per break 2.30 to 2.51 pooled and 2.30 to 2.47 per mouse. The span from the day-1 task session to the sensory-mapping session is 24.21 to 25.71 days across readings (24 mice; VG1-GC#125 has no day-1 session). Measured values are reading (1a), pooled, first sensory session, inclusive. Seven gaps enclose a missing task session; leaving them out changes no match. One break, of VG1-GC#85 between task sessions 4 and 5, lasts 16 days and encloses no missing task session; it makes the s.d. of break lengths 1.7 against the paper's 0.7. Without it the days per break are 2.14 +/- 0.72 pooled, close to the paper's 2.3 +/- 0.7, so the paper may have left it out or counted it otherwise; the means match either way.

outcomes.statement: Across the population the response rate to the tone rose over training, from about 0.55 in task session 1 to about 0.85 in task session 15 (median over mice).
outcomes.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 2; Figure 3c, top panel
outcomes.quote: The response rate to the sound cue tended to increase overall (∼0.55 in task training session 1 to ∼0.85 in task training session 15; median)
outcomes.notes: Median response rate over mice is 0.556 in session 1 and 0.856 in session 15 from the outcome labels (reading a), 0.559 and 0.859 from the 5 kHz lever (reading b), both within tolerance; the 15 medians rise with session (Spearman rho 0.757, p 0.0011).

outcomes.statement: The population success rate stayed roughly constant across the 15 task sessions.
outcomes.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 2; Figure 3c, middle panel
outcomes.quote: while the success rate seemed to be constant as a whole ( Fig. 3c )
outcomes.notes: The criterion's two readings of "constant" disagree. The session-15 median success rate is 27% (labels, 0.485 to 0.616) or 31% (reward TTLs, 0.492 to 0.645) above the session-1 median, so reading (a), within 10%, fails; the 15 medians show no monotonic trend (Spearman rho 0.257, p 0.355 with labels; 0.232, p 0.405 with rewards), so reading (b) holds. The criterion blocks the claim when the readings differ. For contrast the response rate rose 54% over the same sessions. The paper gives no test or bound for "constant"; the question is recorded under findings.

outcomes.statement: Hierarchical clustering (Ward's method) of the session-by-session T_pull_final divides the mice into two clusters, A with 7 mice and B with 18.
outcomes.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 2; Figure 3d and 3e legends
outcomes.quote: The hierarchical clustering revealed that mice could be divided into two clusters in terms of T pull_final ( Fig. 3d ).
outcomes.notes: Ward clustering of the 15 T_pull_final values per mouse gives clusters of 7 and 18 under all three ways of filling the 11 missing sessions, with the same 7 mice in cluster A (VG1-GC#105, VG1-GC#48, VG1-GC#51, VG1-GC#53, VG1-GC#61, VG1-GC#63, VG1-GC#66). Clustering the 14 session-to-session differences gives 3 or 4 against 21 or 22, so only the reading with the values themselves matches.

outcomes.statement: Mice of cluster A had high success rates in the early sessions (about session 5), which led to a high T_pull_final that was often maintained into the late sessions.
outcomes.quote: Mice belonging to one cluster (cluster A) showed high success rates in the early sessions (∼5) leading to high T pull_final which were often maintained even in the late sessions.
outcomes.notes: Cluster A's median success rate exceeds cluster B's in sessions 1 to 5 (0.649 against 0.539 with labels, Mann-Whitney p 0.244) and in session 5 (0.749 against 0.558, p 0.064), and with reward TTLs likewise. Its median T_pull_final exceeds B's in sessions 11 to 15 (0.28 against 0.08 s) and in session 15 (0.30 against 0.075 s). Part (2) follows largely from naming A as the cluster with the higher mean T_pull_final. The claim lists fig3c-success-rate-constant under depends_on for the definition of the success rate; that claim is blocked for its judgement of "constant", not for the measure, so this claim is tested.

outcomes.statement: Mice of cluster B rarely reached a high T_pull_final, but in the late sessions their response and success rates were similar to those of cluster A.
outcomes.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 2; Figure 3e; Figure S1c
outcomes.quote: Mice belonging to the other cluster (cluster B) rarely achieved a high T pull_final , while they accomplished a response rate and success rate similar to the cluster A mice in the late sessions ( Fig. 3e , Fig. S1).
outcomes.notes: Cluster B never reached 400 ms (A in 23.8% of its mouse-sessions) and was above the overall median of 0.10 s in 20.5% of its mouse-sessions (A 82.2%), so the T_pull_final part holds. Late response rates are similar under both readings of "similar" (sessions 11 to 15, A 0.802 and B 0.732, p 0.423, 8.7% apart; session 15, 1.4% apart). For the success rate the two readings of "similar" differ; Mann-Whitney p is 0.58 to 0.82 in every case, but the medians are more than 10% apart with the outcome labels (12.8% over sessions 11 to 15, 16.1% in session 15) and with reward TTLs in session 15 (17.1%), cluster B being the higher; they are within 10% only with reward TTLs over sessions 11 to 15 (9.2%). The criterion blocks the claim when the readings of "similar" differ, and they agree under only one of the four combinations of the success measure and the late sessions, so the claim is blocked. In round 1 it was recorded as reproduced on that one combination; the verifier judged it blocked, and the outcome was changed. The depends_on entry for fig3c-success-rate-constant is treated as for fig3e-cluster-a-high-tpull. The paper gives no test or bound for "similar"; the question is recorded under findings.

outcomes.statement: Fluorescence signal degradation across imaging sessions was not observed.
outcomes.source: Methods, Acquisition of wide-field one-photon image, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: The total power of excitation lights (blue and violet) was set at ∼10 mW and the fluorescent signal degradation across imaging sessions was not observed.
outcomes.notes: Neither reading finds a significant decline. Raw blue fluorescence within the ROI masks, median over time (F_B0); median per-mouse Spearman rho -0.191 (negative in 17 of 25), Wilcoxon p 0.221; session 15 over session 1 median ratio 1.052 (22 mice). The same as the session mean; rho -0.147, p 0.221, ratio 1.043. S.d. of corrected dF/F; median rho 0.022, p 0.840; ratio 0.903. Per ROI without correction for 44 tests, 2 ROIs show a nominal F_B0 decline and 1 an increase; for the s.d., 5 decline and 9 increase. The files hold no raw ROI fluorescence series (processing/ophys holds only dFF, dFF_B, dFF_V and the ROI masks), so the stack is used, as the criterion says. In four sessions read frame by frame (VG1-GC#105 and VG1-GC#116, days 1 and 15) the 160-frame F_B0 is within 0.01% to 0.95% of the all-frame median (the 8 frames of round 1, 0.34% to 1.93%); its sampling s.d. is 1.21% (8 frames, 1.65%) against a median across-session s.d. of 7.8% within a mouse, so sampling noise is about 2% of the across-session variance (8 frames, 4.5%). The session-15 over session-1 ratios of the two mice are 1.076 and 0.868 from every frame and 1.083 and 0.871 from the blocks. In round 1, with 8 frames, reading (a) gave median rho -0.207, p 0.178.
deviations: F_B0 and the session mean are taken over 16 evenly spaced blocks of 10 consecutive blue frames (160 of 54000), not over every frame; reading every frame of every session does not fit the time limit. The error of the subsample is measured on four sessions read frame by frame.

outcomes.statement: MesoNet-inferred skull landmarks used to register the Allen CCF agreed with manual annotations of three representative sessions from each of the 25 mice (75 sessions).
outcomes.quote: We validated the accuracy of this method by comparing the MesoNet-based skull-landmark annotations with the manual annotations, based on three representative sessions from each of the 25 animals ( Fig. 4a,b ).
outcomes.notes: The manual skull-landmark annotations are not in the dataset. The NWB files' analysis group holds only atlas_to_data_transform (all 495 files), and the dandiset holds only NWB files (495) and MP4 videos (1343). The notebook lists the other places the dandiset and the paper name. The repositories BraiDyn-BC/bdbc-data-pipeline (commit ab50b17), bdbc-nwb-packager (0170a1c), bdbc-nwb-explorer (309c5fb) and bdbc-session-explorer (58089f2) hold 16, 36, 19 and 17 files, none of them annotations (the one path naming validation, bdbc_nwb_packager/tracking/validation.py, is code). The Google Drive folder in the dandiset's related resources holds five notebooks (001 Opening NWB files to 005 Data storage). The Matsuzaki lab data platform the dandiset names as a variant form of the dataset holds the folder /Repository/BraiDyn-BC_CuedLeverPull/ (17.0 TB, locked); its API answers the request for the folder's file list with HTTP 403, permission denied, so whether it holds the annotations could not be checked.

outcomes.statement: In the sensory-mapping sessions, visual stimulation of the left eye evoked the strongest activity in the right occipital cortex, at VISp in the registered atlas.
outcomes.quote: Visual stimuli to the left eye of mice elicited prominent activity in the right occipital cortex ( Dräger 1975 ; Grinvald et al. 1986 ; Schuett, Bonhoeffer, and Hübener 2002 ) corresponding to VISp (primary visual area) in the atlas.
outcomes.notes: Over the first sensory-mapping session of each of 25 mice, the 10 Hz flash train (trial code 1) evokes its largest normalized mean response in right VISp (0.95, right VISpm 0.93; 0.94 and 0.92 with the pre-stimulus baseline subtracted). With the stim_visual TTL, present in 19 sessions, right VISp is also largest (0.96). Per mouse right VISp is the top ROI in 8 to 11 mice and right VISpm about as often.
deviations: Only the ROI reading was run. The pixel-map reading needs 60 to 120 frames around each of about 30 stimuli per modality for 25 sessions; a spread frame takes about 0.3 s to reach over the network, which does not fit the time limit with the other claims.
In 6 of 25 first sessions there is no stim_visual channel; there the visual train is on the stim_whisker channel and coded 1, so the code-1 reading uses all 25 mice and the channel reading 19.

outcomes.statement: Vibration of the right whisker pad evoked a robust response in the left barrel cortex (SSp-bfd), with marked laterality.
outcomes.quote: Tactile stimuli to the right whisker pad elicited a robust response in the left SSp-bfd, a primary sensory cortex for processing whisker-related sensory information with marked hemispheric laterality
outcomes.notes: Trial code 3 (25 mice) and the stim_whisker channel over the 19 sessions with three channels evoke their largest mean response in left SSp-bfd (0.87 and 0.99; 0.83 and 0.96 with baseline), above right SSp-bfd (0.55 and 0.66), and left exceeds right SSp-bfd in every mouse (25 of 25, 19 of 19). Over all 25 first sessions the stim_whisker channel carries the visual train in six of them; it still peaks in left SSp-bfd (0.83), and left exceeds right in 19 of 25 mice. Left SSp-bfd is the top ROI in 15 or 16 mice.
deviations: The files do not name the trial codes. Code 3 is on the stim_whisker channel in the 19 sessions with three channels and on the stim_auditory channel in the other six; the code reading, the channel over the 19 sessions, and the channel over all 25 are shown and agree.

outcomes.statement: White-noise stimulation evoked spreading activity that included a multimodal sensory area in the parietal cortex.
outcomes.quote: Auditory stimuli evoked spreading activity, including a multimodal sensory area in the parietal cortex
outcomes.notes: With trial code 2 and the stim_auditory channel over the 19 sessions with three channels (the same onsets), and with the channel over all 25 first sessions, under both baselines, the 80th-percentile region of the mean map spans 9 ROIs and includes left VISa, a posterior parietal ROI (no PTLp ROI exists), so the criterion is met. The evidence is weak. A region of 9 of 44 ROIs always holds more than one ROI, and a random set of 9 ROIs includes one of the 4 parietal ROIs with probability 0.61. The mean map spans 0.17 to 0.83 at most; under code 2 trunk and limb somatosensory ROIs are on top (0.77 to 0.83), and on the channel over all 25 sessions with the baseline left VISpm and VISam are level with them (0.68 to 0.69). The code-2 response of left VISa is larger at the true onsets than at onsets shifted by 3 or 6 s in 10 of 19 mice (median contrast 0.0118 against -0.0096 to -0.0001), and the left AUDs response in 11 of 19. Over all 25 sessions the stim_auditory channel carries code 3, a tactile stimulus, in six. Whether the criterion should compare with a null is asked of a reader (questions/kondo-2025.yaml).
deviations: Only the ROI reading was run (see fig4d-visual-map). Code 2 exists only in 19 first sessions; the six sessions of the earliest cohort have two stimulus types.

outcomes.statement: The mice showed no sign of the aberrant short-duration, large-amplitude calcium transients reported in some transgenic lines; no cluster of transients had high prominence (> 0.1 dF/F) and narrow width (< 0.5 s).
outcomes.source: Technical Validation, paragraph 3; Figure S2b legend
outcomes.quote: High prominence (> 0.1 in Δ F / F ) and narrow width (< 0.5 s) of the transients were not detected in each animal (right).
outcomes.notes: In 1200 runs (25 mice, 6 ROIs covering the readings of frontal and retrosplenial, 2 signals, 2 detection thresholds, raw or z-scored features) no K-means centre has prominence above 0.1 with width below 0.5 s. The highest centre prominence is 0.436 and the narrowest width of a centre with the higher prominence is 0.34 s, in different centres. Median 727 to 1844 transients per ROI depending on the threshold.
deviations: The peak detection and the K-means settings (scipy.signal.find_peaks; scikit-learn KMeans with 10 initialisations, random_state 0) are not given in the paper; the claims file names find_peaks.

outcomes.statement: DeepLabCut keypoints differed from manual annotations only by minor errors on validation frames (192 frames from 25 mice for the body and face cameras, 190 for the eye).
outcomes.quote: Comparison of DeepLabCut model-based keypoint annotations with manual annotations showed minor errors, validating the quality of our models ( Fig. 5a-c ).
outcomes.notes: The manual annotations of the validation frames are not in the dataset, which holds only the DeepLabCut estimates and likelihoods, nor in the four BraiDyn-BC repositories or the Google Drive folder named above; the Matsuzaki lab data platform is access-restricted (see fig4ab-landmark-validation).

outcomes.statement: The lever-tip position tracked from the body video correlated highly with the encoder lever position, R = 0.98 +/- 0.02 (mean +/- s.d.).
outcomes.quote: Moreover, the lever tip position estimated from the videography showed a markedly high correlation (0.98 ± 0.02; mean ± s.d.) with the encoder-based lever position ( Fig. 5e,f ).
outcomes.notes: Over 356 task sessions with body keypoints and at least one successful trial, the mean Pearson R of the lever-tip keypoint y position with the encoder lever is 0.978 to 0.985 over sessions and 0.977 to 0.985 over per-mouse means across all readings (main reading 0.981 +/- 0.021). 4 sessions are below 0.9 (min 0.748). Per-mouse means are printed.
deviations: The lever-tip keypoint is rightbartip, which the paper's linked code describes as the tip of the lever (bdbc-nwb-explorer data/body_video.csv); the NWB files give no description.

outcomes.statement: The right forepaw, which pulls the lever, correlated with the lever position (R = 0.49 +/- 0.23), and the left forepaw did not (R = 0.05 +/- 0.19), over 354 task sessions from 25 mice.
outcomes.quote: We found this is exactly the case, based on the 354 task-recording sessions of our dataset that successfully included upper-body videos ( Fig. 5d-f ; right forepaw, 0.49 ± 0.23; left forepaw, 0.05 ± 0.19; mean±s.d., n = 354 sessions from 25 animals
outcomes.notes: The right forepaw's mean R is 0.472 to 0.498 and the left forepaw's 0.052 to 0.066 with R as computed (0.147 to 0.161 as absolute values), within 0.49 +/- 0.23 and 0.05 +/- 0.19 under every reading; right exceeds left in all 25 mice. The session count, an exact expected value, is 356 against 354. The dataset has 357 task sessions with body keypoints (the paper says 355), one of them (VG1-GC#63 day 6) without a successful trial; the 7 task sessions without body keypoints are those noted "no behavioral videos are available". Two of the 357 (VG1-GC#119 days 2 and 4) are noted "face video is not available"; leaving them out gives the paper's 355 and 354 (printed), but the paper does not say it did, so this is a possible account, not a finding. The pawrest keypoint (leftbartip) correlates with the lever at R 0.40 to 0.45, though the Methods describe the pawrest as immobile.

outcomes.statement: In the example session, the forepaws and the nose began moving before lever-pull onset, and the jaw and pupil diameter changed after it.
outcomes.quote: While some body parts, such as forepaws and nose, began moving before the lever-pull onset, others, including jaw and pupil diameter, moved afterward at least in this session.
outcomes.notes: No reading holds, and the onset rule of the criterion is not a valid test. On synthetic trial averages without movement the rule gives an onset before 0 in 66% (white noise) to 85% (smooth noise) of runs at 2 s.d. and 28% to 58% at 3 s.d.; a variant that requires the crossing to last 100 ms gives 3% for white noise but 42% for smooth noise at 2 s.d. In the data, under every rule (2 or 3 s.d., with or without the 100 ms requirement), both forms of the displacement trace and both pull sets, every keypoint's grand onset is -0.5 s, the first sample after the baseline window, so the onsets do not show the order. The grand traces show it without a rule; the jaw displacement of the mean position is 3.74 pixels at -0.3 s, 6.41 at -0.2 s and 19.13 at 0 s, against a baseline of 0.43 +/- 0.27, so in the mean over 352 or 353 sessions the jaw moves before the pull; the forepaws (2.55 and 2.89 pixels at -0.3 s) and the nose (1.48) move before it too, and the pupil diameter rises from 56.65 +/- 0.09 to 56.93 pixels at -0.1 s. The full order holds in no session, and the jaw has an onset before 0 in 99% or more of them. The paper states the order for one session it does not identify, so the claims file blocks the claim when no reading holds. Whether the criterion should judge onsets another way is asked of a reader (questions/kondo-2025.yaml); the example session is asked of the authors (findings).
deviations: The criterion's "displacement ... trial average" was run both as the trial average of each trial's displacement and as the displacement of the trial-averaged position; they agree.
Pupil diameters that are not finite, not positive or above 300 pixels are set missing.

A variant of the onset rule that requires the trace to stay outside the band for at least 100 ms (3 samples) is also shown, an assumption added after the first verification round; it changes no onset of the grand traces. The outcome is blocked under every rule, so it does not rest on this assumption and is not marked assumed.

outcomes.statement: In the example session, MOs activity returned quickly to baseline after the pull, while MOp and the upper-limb and nose somatosensory areas (SSp-ul, SSp-n) stayed slightly above baseline after reward delivery.
outcomes.quote: The secondary motor cortex (MOs) quickly recovered to the baseline level. In contrast, the primary motor (MOp) and somatosensory cortex (SSpul and SSpn) showed slightly higher activity than the baseline level after the reward delivery.
outcomes.notes: In the mean over 356 or 357 sessions, MOs's post-reward value minus baseline (0.0010 to 0.0140) is below those of MOp (0.016 to 0.035), SSp-ul (0.022 to 0.045) and SSp-n (0.008 to 0.027), all above 0, under every window, pull set and hemisphere (reading a). Session by session the full pattern holds in 38% to 60% of sessions, so reading (b), more than half, holds only for the reward-aligned window. The paper states it for one example session. The criterion does not test the statement's "returned quickly to baseline", and in the mean over sessions that part does not show; MOs stays above its baseline in every window, by 0.0131 to 0.0140 in the reward-aligned one, about half of SSp-n's 0.0244 to 0.0266. Whether the criterion should test it is asked of a reader (questions/kondo-2025.yaml).

outcomes.statement: In the example session, OB, RSPagl, AUDs and VISp had activity time courses that closely matched pupil dilation.
outcomes.quote: Other sensory-related areas (OB, olfactory bulb; RSPagl, retrosplenial area, lateral agranular part; AUDs, secondary auditory areas; VISp, primary visual area) showed activity traces that shared time courses closely matching the pupil dilation.
outcomes.notes: No reading holds. In the mean over 355 or 356 sessions OB follows the pupil (r 0.95 to 0.96 with pupil against 0.62 to 0.64 with lever), but RSPagl (0.32 to 0.43 against 0.95 to 0.96), AUDs and VISp follow the lever more closely than the pupil, in each hemisphere and pull set, and the full pattern holds in at most 1.4% of sessions. As the paper states it for an unidentified example session, the claims file blocks the claim.

outcomes.statement: Cortical activity varied less across trials after lever-pull onset than before it.
outcomes.quote: The data also revealed a decrease in activity variability after the lever-pull onset, exemplifying how stereotypic movements like lever-pull constrain cortical activity.
outcomes.notes: In the mean over sessions the across-trial s.d. of dF/F is lower after lever-pull onset than in the second before it in 44 of 44 ROIs (43 for valid pulls over 0 to 3 s), Wilcoxon p below 1e-11, median ratio 0.71 to 0.79; most ROIs are lower in 82% to 96% of sessions.

findings.statement: In all 495 NWB files ImagingPlane_blue states an excitation_lambda of 405 nm and ImagingPlane_UV 470 nm, while their descriptions, the series descriptions and the Methods give the reverse (blue 470 or 473 nm, violet 405 nm). The data fit the names; in four sessions read frame by frame the stack named blue is about three times as bright as the one named UV and follows dFF_B, and the UV stack's frame-to-frame changes follow dFF_V. In three of the four sessions dFF_B carries a lever-pull response that dFF_V lacks; in the fourth (VG1-GC#116 day 1) neither does.

The lever and the other sensor channels are stored with unit "a.u." and description "no description"; the paper's code gives the lever in mm, the environmental sensors in hPa, ppm, % and degrees C, and the meaning of state_task codes (bdbc-nwb-explorer data/daq.csv). The values fit mm (lever range about -0.4 to 4.3).

The sensory-mapping trial tables code each stimulus as stim_modality 1, 2 or 3 with no description of the codes. In the six sessions of mice VG1-GC#51, VG1-GC#52, VG1-GC#53, VG1-GC#54, VG1-GC#60 and VG1-GC#61 there is no stim_visual channel; the stim_whisker channel carries a 10 Hz train coded 1 whose map peaks in right VISp, the stim_auditory channel carries code 3 whose map peaks in left SSp-bfd, and there is no third stimulus, although the session description names three. In the other 27 sessions code 1 is on stim_visual, 2 on stim_auditory and 3 on stim_whisker.

In the 27 sensory-mapping sessions with three stimuli the trials run in the order code 1, 2, 3, which by the channel names is visual, auditory, tactile; the Methods give the fixed order visual, tactile, auditory.

Reward TTL onsets outnumber the trials labelled success in 205 of 364 task sessions (by 1 to 60, median 1) and are fewer in one; the down-sampled reward series differs from the labels in some sessions too (by -35 to 12). The success rate depends on which is counted.
The down-sampled keypoint series (processing/downsampled/*_video_keypoints) keep a confidence array of the 100 Hz video length next to 30 Hz data, so the two cannot be paired.

The pupil diameter series contain values that are infinite or far wider than the 300-pixel eye video (1e5 pixels and more), in a median 0.14% of the 30 Hz frames per session and above 5% in 10 of 356 sessions (up to 63%).
357 task sessions have body-camera keypoints, against 355 in the paper, and 356 of them have a successful trial, against the paper's 354 analysed sessions.

The session-initial T_pull equals the previous session's T_pull_final minus 100 ms (floored at 0) in 219 of 332 pairs of consecutive sessions; in the others it is often 0 or 50 ms after a final of 50 to 150 ms. The Methods state the minus-100-ms rule.

Four sensory-mapping sessions (VG1-GC#48, VG1-GC#63, VG1-GC#66 and VG1-GC#73) hold 36000 frames (20 min) where the Methods give 15 min (27000 frames); one task session holds 45413 frames, noted in the file.
The paper's Data Records describe two TIFF stacks per session; the dandiset holds the motion-corrected stacks inside the NWB files (widefield_blue and widefield_UV) and no TIFF files.

The manual skull-landmark annotations (75 sessions) and the manual keypoint annotations of the DeepLabCut validation frames behind Figures 4a,b and 5a-c are not in the dataset or the linked repositories, so those validations cannot be repeated. The Matsuzaki lab data platform that the dandiset names as a variant form of the dataset is access-restricted, so it could not be searched.
The trial tables give T_pull (pull_duration_for_success) values of 0.0 s in 10783 of 48549 trials (157 sessions), where the Methods give a 1 ms start.

Raw tone TTL onsets outnumber the trials in most task sessions, usually by one or two, and by more than 10 in nine sessions (up to 145, VG1-GC#78 day 4); the down-sampled tone series rises once per trial in every session.

paper_notes.statement: Question for the paper's authors. Which task session is the example of Figure 6, and how were the movement onsets, the match of area traces with the pupil, and the drop in variability judged? Over all sessions the jaw moves before lever-pull onset and RSPagl, AUDs and VISp follow the lever more than the pupil, so the Figure 6b statements cannot be checked without the session.

Question for the paper's authors. What test or bound supports "the success rate seemed to be constant" (Figure 3c)? The medians show no monotonic trend (Spearman p 0.36), but the session-15 median is 27% above session 1's.

Question for the paper's authors. What test or bound supports "a response rate and success rate similar to the cluster A mice in the late sessions" (Figure 3e, S1), and are successes counted from the outcome labels or the reward deliveries? The late success rates do not differ by Mann-Whitney test (p 0.58 to 0.82), but cluster B's median is 9% to 17% above cluster A's.

entries.name: kondo-2025
entries.title: Wide-field calcium imaging and behaviour in the BraiDyn-BC lever-pull task (Kondo et al. 2025)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Kondo, Sehara, Harukuni, Aoki et al. (2025) on dandiset 001425, which holds wide-field calcium imaging, behavioural sensors and video keypoints from 25 mice over 15 sessions of a cued lever-pull task, with resting-state and sensory-mapping sessions. It checks the session and cohort counts, the learning curves and the clustering of mice by required pull duration, the stability of the fluorescence, the sensory maps, the absence of aberrant transients, the correlation of video keypoints with the lever, and the pull-aligned activity and movements.
